newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urged to focus health efforts on common killers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urged to focus health efforts on common killers.

text.p: The United States should focus its international health efforts on the prevention of common infectious diseases such as malaria and tuberculosis rather than diverting scarce resources to the "disease du jour," Congress heard on Wednesday.

While dangerous new disease strains made for great movies and books, they could produce shortsighted public policies, Sally Shelton-Colby, assistant administrator of the Agency for International Development, told a House of Representatives committee.
"Acute outbreaks of exotic viral diseases such as Ebola and threats of plague have dominated the headlines," she said.

But deaths from high-visibility diseases like Ebola had numbered in the hundreds, while every year 17 million people died worldwide as a result of routine infectious diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis and dehydration from diarrhoea, she added.
Shelton-Colby noted that the United States was a major contributor to the emergency response to the Ebola outbreak in Zaire and played a smaller role in the plague panic in India.

"However, we strongly believe that responding to emergencies should be a last recourse, not a first, and we worry that fundamental prevention and control efforts may inadvertently be undermined by a diversion of resources to whatever has most recently appeared on CNN," she said.
Nevertheless, members of the House International Relations Committee appeared captivated by a display of U.S. Army equipment for responding to an outbreak of a deadly disease.

Several left their podium seats for a closer look as an army officer explained the isolation stretchers fully sealed in large transparent plastic tents with double vents to allow doctors to work on a patient without becoming contaminated.
Two young soldiers modelled head-to-toe bright yellow filter outfits complete with oxygen intakes, while an inflated bulky blue "hot suit" which is hooked up to an oxygen tank hung nearby.
The equipment was supplied by the U.S. Army Medical Research Centre at Fort Detrick, Maryland, where the military researches and develops vaccines and antidotes for biological and chemical agents.

Dr. David Heymann, of the World Health Organisation, told the committee that Ebola and pneumonic plague caused relatively few -- but highly fatal infections -- and great concern internationally when they emerged.

But he said the spectrum of infectious diseases included more common illnesses such as dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease that hit more than 500,000 in Latin America in 1995-96, and AIDS which killed 1.5 million adults and children worldwide last year.

"If global surveillance and control systems such as WHO is establishing had been in place and functioning during the 1970s, the magnitude of the AIDS problem would probably not be so severe," he said.
Heymann said infectious diseases were increasing throughout the world because of weakened public health systems and were linked to behaviour, deforestation, climate change and social upheaval.
